newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Adare's Lynch call for private investor tax breaks.
newsitem.headline: Adare's Lynch call for private investor tax breaks.

text.p: Irish firms will bypass the local stock exchange and go straight to the larger capital pools of London and the U.S. unless efforts are made to support a private investment culture, Adare finance director Peter Lynch said.
"There is little incentive to have an Irish personal or corporate tax residence and there is nothing more mobile than capital," Lynch told the Leinster Society of Chartered Accountants on Wednesday.
He also said that the Irish stock market could face "a stampede of dwarves" as secondline stocks exited the market unless attempts are made to encourage private investors.
Lynch said that there are no natural buyers for secondliners unless specific secondline funds are established, assuming all fund fund managers act in the same way -- to maximise returns.
In a recession, foreign buyers would sell secondline stocks in order to protect their liquidity and would take a significant mark down to exit, he said.

"If it is not commercially sensible for institutions to take up the slack in Irish secondliners, then the only other candidate is the private investor," Lynch, formerly managing director at Riada Stockbrokers, said.
Otherwise, the price/earnings ratios of secondline stocks, already only 65 percent of the UK equivalent, fall.
This prevents overseas buying and Irish secondline stocks become takeover targets, candidates for management buyouts or likely to consider moving to a higher-rated market.

Lynch said the government should consider a number of possible tax breaks such as the provision of interest relief for borrowing to invest in quoted stock and income tax breaks for investment in primary issues.
He also suggested enhancing the structure of special investment accounts and the abolition of income tax payable on the exercise of options.

"Middle level entrepreneurs are labouring in an environment hostile to risk taking and wealth creation through the medium of public companies and will tire of promoting illiquid stocks in a peripheral, illiquid market where income charges, capital accumulation taxes and the cost of risk is too high," he said.
